name: specification
intent: Encapsulate a business rule as a first-class predicate object over a candidate type, so that rules can be named, reused, combined with AND/OR/NOT and tested independently of the code that applies them.
problem: A single business rule - who is eligible for a discount, which invoice goes to collection, which cargo fits which container - has to be applied in several places at once: in-memory validation, selection from a collection or repository, bulk update, and the construction of an object that must meet the rule. Written inline, the condition is duplicated at every call site, the copies drift apart, and the rule is invisible to domain experts and untestable outside the use case that contains it.
context: Domain models and enterprise applications where the rules are stable domain concepts rather than configuration data; where a rule is reused by more than one consumer or combined with other rules; and where the same rule may have to run both in memory (validation, object creation) and inside a store query (selection, bulk update). It also applies outside a persistence backdrop whenever criteria must be named, composed and tested in isolation.
benefits: One named home per rule: the condition is stated once and shared by validation, selection, bulk update and object creation instead of being re-inlined at each call site.
Composable by Boolean algebra: leaf rules combine with AND/OR/NOT into new rules without editing the existing ones, so the rule set stays open for extension and closed for modification.
Independently testable: a specification has no collaborators and no side effects, so each rule is exercised against boundary candidates without a fixture, database or mock.
Domain vocabulary: rules are named after domain concepts (Overdue, EligibleForDiscount, MeetsStorageRequirements) and become part of the ubiquitous language, readable to domain experts.

One rule definition can feed both an in-memory check and a translated store query, which is how validation and selection are kept from disagreeing about what the rule means - provided the translation is faithful.
Immutable and shareable: a specification carries only its parameters, so it can be cached, passed across layers and reused by concurrent callers.

Decoupled responsibilities: requirements, evaluation and validation become separate jobs, so route selection, container assignment and portfolio membership can all be phrased as the same kind of object.
tradeoffs: Indirection before reuse: for a rule used at one call site a plain function or inline condition is shorter; the interface, combinator types and translation machinery only pay for themselves once rules are shared, composed or reviewed.

Double definition risk: a rule that runs both in memory and as a translated store query exists twice; the object and the SQL fragment drift silently, and the failure surfaces as a query selecting a different set than the validation accepts.

Performance boundary: in-memory evaluation means loading candidates and filtering in the application, while pushing rules into the store requires a translator, index-aware predicates and care with lazy associations - an unfaithful or navigation-heavy specification can trigger an N+1 query.

The pattern fights persistence ignorance by design: as soon as a specification knows how to become a query (toSql, toPredicate, Criteria types), domain rule objects depend on the store's API or on a visitor somebody must maintain.

Boolean semantics are easy to get wrong: null candidates, short-circuit order, exceptions escaping from a predicate, negation of a three-valued condition and stateful specifications all produce objects that are not predicates at all.

Rule explosion: one class per trivial comparison, or a generic field/operator interpreter, turns the domain model into an accidental rules engine that is harder to read than the conditions it replaced.
Rule parameters are easy to hide: a specification constructor that reads configuration or a clock makes the rule implicit again, so the same object answers differently in test and production.
Every new rule is a new type (and often a new file, test class and review), which is more process weight than a changed if-condition.

Crossover pollution: mixing a domain specification (IsSatisfiedBy returning bool) with a query envelope (Expression<Func<T,bool>> with ordering, pagination, includes) conflates two concerns and makes the spec no longer a pure predicate - the composite cannot be reasoned about as Boolean logic alone.

participants.responsibility: Declares the single evaluation operation over the candidate type - isSatisfiedBy(candidate), is_satisfied_by, test, operator() - and, in the classic form, the combinators and/or/not that return new specifications.
The domain object, value or projected row that is tested. A specification is meaningless without the type it constrains, and a narrow candidate type keeps the rule reusable and cheap to test.

Concrete rule that evaluates one condition: hard-coded leaves express a fixed criterion in code, parameterized leaves hold the values that vary (thresholds, dates, categories, identifiers) as constructor parameters.
And/Or/Not nodes that hold child specifications and combine their results, forming a tree (Composite plus Interpreter structure) that can be evaluated, traversed, logged or translated.
Applies a specification: filters in-memory candidates, guards an operation, or hands the specification to a repository that turns it into a store query.

Optional role that walks the specification tree and emits the store representation (SQL, Criteria, expression tree). Keeping it outside the rule objects is what preserves domain persistence ignorance.

use_cases: Eligibility and policy decisions: is this customer eligible for the loyalty discount, may this vessel carry this cargo, does this trade require a risk review.
Selection with a reusable criterion: the canonical example — lists the invoices that are overdue, have had notices sent and are not already with the collection agency.
Repository query composition: named specifications translated into WHERE clauses or Criteria, so a repository exposes a few generic find methods instead of dozens of ad-hoc query methods.
Validation before an operation: check that a candidate satisfies a policy without pushing the rule into the candidate or into the caller (cargo-to-container fit, account eligible for a transfer).
Building to order: the specification defines the target and a factory or selector derives an object that satisfies it (a route specification driving a route selector).
Bulk updates and mass operations: select the set of entities a rule matches and apply one operation to them (bulk discount, bulk archive, send-to-collection) while the rule stays in the model.
Test data and simulation: the same specification generates candidate objects that satisfy a rule, so tests and simulations reuse the production criterion.

CQRS read-model projection gates: a specification determines whether a domain event should update a given read-model record (e.g., OnlyActiveCustomerReadModel updated when ActiveCustomerSpec is satisfied).

Compliance and screening rules: anti-money-laundering Know-Your-Customer (KYC) checks, trade sanction screening and Know-Your-Business (KYB) eligibility as composable specifications assembled from regulated criteria.

Event-sourcing filter predicates: replay-only event streams through a specification so that projections or process managers consume only the events relevant to their domain (e.g., only OrderPlaced events matching OrderForDigitalGoodsSpec).

Fintech fraud detection and risk scoring: composeable specifications evaluate transaction patterns against regulatory thresholds (e.g., transaction velocity, geolocation anomalies, amount outliers) in real-time payment processing pipelines.

Multi-step workflow preconditions: specification gates on workflow state machines (e.g., Hepsiburada OMS order address-change blocked unless CountryCodeIsTurkeySpec.And(ShippingMethodIsHepsiJetSpec).And(TenantIsHepsiburadaSpec) passes), where composite specifications model complex business rules readable to non-technical stakeholders.

Role-based access control (RBAC) at the query level: specifications encapsulate permission rules that filter data access across repositories, enabling granular row-level security without scattering permission checks throughout the codebase.

Dynamic search filters over relational stores: Spring Data JPA's Specification<T> and JpaSpecificationExecutor express composable predicates over entities via the JPA Criteria API and reuse them across repositories — the official reference documents the API as based on Eric Evans' specification concept, making it the most widely deployed production use of the pattern.

Catalog and basket queries in Microsoft's eShopOnWeb reference application: typed Ardalis.Specification classes define the criteria and a repository executes them, the canonical .NET composition of repository.find(spec) instead of ad-hoc query methods.
avoid_when: The rule is checked at exactly one call site and never combined: write the condition inline or pass a plain lambda - an extra type adds nothing.

The rule is a property of the object itself (always true of that object when it is valid): put it inside the entity or aggregate as a guard; a specification is for external constraints over candidates.
Rules must be edited by business users at runtime without a deployment: that is a rules engine or an external DSL problem, not a specification object.
The criteria are really query mechanics (index hints, join strategies, report filters): model them as a query object or builder in the persistence layer.
The conditions are throwaway filters for one screen, never reused, never named and never tested separately.
What is being modelled is the object itself rather than a constraint on it - a route built entirely out of route-specification attributes loses the distinction the pattern is about.
Simple CRUD applications where query logic never exceeds one or two fixed filters: the pattern's ceremony exceeds its value.
Ultra-high-performance paths where microseconds matter: specification indirection and expression tree compilation add measurable overhead on hot paths.
anti_patterns: Impure specifications: isSatisfiedBy loads lazy collections, calls services or mutates state, so the rule cannot be reasoned about or tested in isolation.
Rule duplication between the in-memory specification and the SQL/query fragment, letting the two definitions drift apart.
Anemic specification explosion: a class per single comparison, or a Specification of untyped fields and operators, replacing readable domain conditions with ceremonial types.
Using a specification to model the whole object (a route specification carrying every route attribute) - the poor man's frame system Fowler warns about.
Stateful specifications whose result depends on call order, on cached candidate data or on mutated parameters.
Negating an unreliable predicate: a rule that throws or returns null for some candidates is turned into a silently true condition by a Not combinator.

Generic IRepository<T> exposing IQueryable<T>: the repository leaks the ORM's query model, forcing callers to write criteria in LINQ/SQL rather than using named specifications - the abstraction is inverted and the specification pattern's purpose is defeated.

Conflating Expression<Func<T,bool>> with ISpecification<T>: bundling ordering, pagination and Include() clauses into a specification object makes it a query builder, not a predicate - the resulting 'specification' cannot be reasoned about as Boolean algebra and breaks the domain model's ability to use it for in-memory validation.

Client-configured specifications: accepting expression lambdas from calling code turns the specification into a thin delegate wrapper with no domain meaning; different callers implement the same business concept differently, duplicating the problem the pattern was meant to solve.

Repository method proliferation: adding findByX methods to repositories instead of composing specifications forces a many-method repository that is harder to test and maintain than a few generic methods accepting composable specifications.
design_principles: Single responsibility: one specification states one rule, and its only operation answers a question about a candidate.
Open/closed: new criteria arrive as new specifications, combinators or translation visitors; existing rules and their clients stay unchanged.
Composition over inheritance: complex rules are assembled from leaves instead of deepening a hierarchy of condition classes.
Separation of concerns and persistence ignorance: stating a rule, evaluating it against a candidate, and translating it into a store query are distinct responsibilities.
Immutability and side-effect-free functions: a specification is a function of the candidate and must not change itself, the candidate or anything else.
Information hiding: clients see named rules; field access, thresholds and null handling stay inside the leaf.
Dependency inversion: clients depend on the specification abstraction, not on the concrete criteria they will be handed.

Narrow candidate type: restrict the candidate to the minimum interface or type the rule actually needs; this maximises reusability and makes specs testable without constructing full aggregate hierarchies.
Pure predicate contract: isSatisfiedBy returns bool (or Reason/bool pair) and does nothing else; side effects, service calls and state mutation disqualify an object from being a specification.
best_practices: Name specifications after the domain concept they express (Overdue, EligibleForDiscount), not after the implemented comparison (CheckDateLessThan).
Keep specifications immutable and side-effect-free; combinators return new specifications instead of mutating the receiver, so rules can be cached and shared safely across concurrent callers.

Define identity elements — an always-true and an always-false specification — so combinators need no null checks and callers can begin with a neutral rule (Spec.True for progressive narrowing via AND; Spec.False for progressive widening via OR).

Decide the evaluation boundary first: pure in-memory rule, query-translatable rule, or both; if both, keep the translator outside the domain classes and test both paths against the same boundary candidates.
Prefer a plain function for local, single-use rules and promote it to a named specification once it is reused, composed, translated, logged or discussed with domain experts.
Keep the candidate type as narrow as possible (an interface, a projection or an immutable view): it documents what the rule needs and makes the rule testable without constructing whole aggregates.
Test leaves against boundary candidates and composites against truth tables, including short-circuiting, negation and null-candidate cases.
Return a reason, not just a boolean, at the boundary where a rejected candidate must be explained; keep the specification itself a pure predicate and let the caller collect the failing leaves.

In EF Core-backed systems, keep leaf expressions translatable: avoid custom C# methods, ToString() on non-string types, Regex.Match, and complex LINQ inside predicates; verify the generated SQL with logging or a profiler.

Avoid traversing lazy-loaded navigation properties during specification tree traversal — this is the primary source of N+1 queries; use eager loading (Include or split queries) in the adapter layer instead.

In Go or similarly typed functional languages, implement the translator as a visitor interface on each leaf, keep composite glue in one recursive function, and keep leaves in the adapter package so the domain never sees SQL or table names.

For multi-parameter or contextual specifications, prefer factory methods on the type (Customer.EligibleForDiscount(params)) over parameterful constructors to make the domain intent explicit and guide callers toward the correct overload.

In C#/.NET, distinguish clearly between Expression<Func<T,bool>> (for EF Core query translation) and Func<T,bool> (for in-memory evaluation); do not bundle both into one object unless the abstraction explicitly documents the dual contract.

Use Ardalis.Specification or equivalent library for .NET when the full query envelope (Where, Include, OrderBy, Skip, Take) is needed — its ISpecification<T> interface cleanly separates the predicate from the query-shaping concerns.

In Spring Data JPA, use PredicateSpecification (Spring Data JPA 4.0+) for query-type-agnostic composition and fall back to the older Specification<T> interface only when query-type-specific variants (select, update, delete) are required.

Prefer static factory methods for specification construction (CustomerSpecs.isOverdue(), OrderSpecs.hasStatus()) over constructor calls; factories express domain intent (whoAmI) and compose naturally into readable specification chains.

When specifications need to return explanation (which clauses failed), model the return as a Result/Reason type pair rather than throwing exceptions from isSatisfiedBy — exceptions corrupt the Boolean algebra of compositors.

In event-sourced systems, replay filters should be modelled as specifications over event types; this keeps the projection logic declarative and auditable without coupling the domain model to projection infrastructure.

For compliance/regulatory rules (AML, KYC), version specifications with a rule-version identifier so that historical decisions can be audited against the exact specification text that applied at decision time.

Avoid the generic Specification<T>(string field, string op, object value) interpreter form — it shifts domain logic into string-based configuration that is invisible to the compiler, untestable without a database and unreadable to domain experts.
sources: Eric Evans and Martin Fowler, Specifications (original pattern paper, 2003) — The canonical reference. Defines hard-coded, parameterized, and composite forms. Introduces subsumption and partially-satisfied supplemental patterns. Composite Specification uses an Interpreter [GoF] structure. Warns explicitly against using Specification as a 'poor man's frame system' — the rule is not the thing it constrains.
https://martinfowler.com/apsupp/spec.pdf

Clarifies the four canonical use cases: data retrieval, in-memory validation, object creation, bulk updates. Argues domain purity is more valuable than encapsulation and documents why he avoids the pattern for query translation.

related_patterns_notes.strategy: Both encapsulate an algorithm behind an interface. The distinction is intent: Strategy selects among interchangeable algorithms at runtime to optimize or vary behaviour; Specification selects candidates that satisfy a criterion and does not care about execution efficiency. A Strategy answers 'which algorithm do I run?' while a Specification answers 'does this candidate match?'. The Fowler/EVans Specification uses an Interpreter structure internally for composition, which is orthogonal to Strategy's interchangeability contract.
related_patterns_notes.composite: Composite is the structural vehicle for the composite Specification form: leaf specifications are the Component, And/Or/Not nodes are the Composite. The distinction matters because Composite describes part-whole hierarchies (trees where children are parts of parents), while Specification's combinators are purely logical - the composite of two specifications is not a 'bigger specification' in the domain sense, it is a new Boolean expression.
related_patterns_notes.interpreter: The composite Specification form is a direct application of the Interpreter pattern [GoF]: a Boolean expression language with terminal expressions (leaf specs) and combinators (And/Or/Not) that produce new expressions. The GoF Interpreter pattern exists to evaluate sentences in a language; the Specification pattern evaluates truth of a candidate against a domain criterion. Some implementations expose a visitor interface on spec nodes, which is Interpreter's canonical evaluation mechanism.
related_patterns_notes.repository: Repository abstracts data access behind a collection-like interface; Specification is the criterion Repository uses to select. Repository is about where data comes from and how it is persisted; Specification is about what condition the data must satisfy. The two compose naturally: repository.find(spec) is the idiomatic entry point. Do not confuse them - a repository that exposes IQueryable or arbitrary Where clauses is a 'leaky abstraction' (SmellsFinder) that displaces the specification's reuse and testability benefits.
related_patterns_notes.query-object: Fowler's Query Object [PoEAA] is a specialised Interpreter for building database queries programmatically. Query Object is a superset of Specification: a Specification is essentially the 'Criteria' part of a Query Object. Query Object can express arbitrary joins, projections and ordering; Specification expresses only Boolean predicates. Use Query Object when you need to model query structure (joins, grouping, set operations); use Specification when the domain concept is a reusable Boolean business rule.
related_patterns_notes.filter-bus: Filter Bus [ Hohnny/P Schuster ] distributes incoming requests or events to handler functions based on registered predicates; it is the architectural analogue of Specification, where a specification acts as the predicate gate on an event stream. The Filter Bus pattern is how Specifications connect to event-sourcing projection replay.
related_patterns_notes.policy: Policy [PoEAA] encapsulates a rule that may vary at runtime, often encapsulating a process or calculation strategy (discount calculation, routing algorithm). Specification is a narrower predicate - Policy may contain computation and state changes, while Specification returns only Boolean satisfaction and must be side-effect-free. The patterns overlap when a policy is expressed as 'eligible = this specification is satisfied'.
related_patterns_notes.claim-check: Claim Check separates a large message payload from its reference, storing the payload separately and passing only the reference through the message bus. Specification can validate the claim-check reference without deserializing the payload, acting as a content-type gate in event-driven workflows.
related_patterns_notes.cqrs: CQRS separates read and write models; Specifications are a natural fit on the read/query side where composable predicates filter read-model projections. On the write/command side, Specifications can guard command execution (command precondition checks). The separation is clean because a write-side specification often evaluates aggregate invariants (stateful, domain-scoped) while a read-side specification evaluates projection filters (stateless, query-scoped).
related_patterns_notes.rule-engine: Rule Engine externalises business logic into a runtime-executable ruleset editable by non-developers. Specification is an in-code, compile-time-fixed version of the same idea - a named, composable predicate. Specification is appropriate when rules are stable domain concepts that developers author and test; Rule Engine is appropriate when business users must create, modify or version rules without deployment. Specification becomes an accidental Rule Engine when its configuration grows to include runtime parameters, rule prioritisation or conflict resolution.
related_patterns_notes.value-object: Both are immutable, side-effect-free domain constructs. A Value Object describes a quantity or description with no identity; a Specification describes a constraint with no state. Parameterized specifications (threshold values, date ranges, category sets) are often implemented as Value Objects passed to the specification constructor, reinforcing the immutability contract.
related_patterns_notes.side-effect-free-function: This is not a GoF/Evans pattern name but a design principle that underpins Specification. A specification's isSatisfiedBy must be a total pure function: same candidate always produces the same result, no state is modified, no external calls are made. Violating this turns the specification into an impure procedure that cannot be tested in isolation, cached, or composed reliably.
related_patterns_notes.closure-of-operations: The closure property of Boolean algebra - AND, OR, NOT of Specifications return Specifications - is what makes the composable Specification work. This is the mathematical foundation that guarantees the pattern's open/closed behaviour: new behaviour comes from composing existing behaviour, not modifying it.
